catalog_quote: [p.125] Earlier phonemic analysis of Magindanao (Eck, Ms) has shown that four vowels, /i, ɨ, a, u/, can be contrasted in stressed and unstressed antepenultimate and ultimate syllables. This paper discusses the vowel contrasts in stressed and unstressed penultimate syllables. ... [p.126] Both words in the first example are members of the V-initial, ultimately stressed group of stems, and the significant factors governing this class of words has yet to be determined. ... [p.128] In normal conversational stress patterns (as opposed to the stress patterns of commands, repetitions, and exclamations), /ɨ/ is not found in stressed penultimate syllables. Therefore, only three vowels can be contrasted in this environment: /i,a,u/. ... [pp.129-130] These patterns are so noticeable that the original analysis of the data (Eck, Ms) posited that all of the stressless N2 phones were actually allophone…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all deciding passages (Eck 1974 pp.125, 126, 128, 129-130, 130 fn.2) confirmed verbatim in the held page-image PDF, which is complete (pp.125-131). (2) The coding 'lexical' rests on a short 1974 SIL phonemic work paper by the primary field linguist, who lists stress as a phoneme and explicitly retracts his own earlier predictable (penult-unless-/ɨ/) analysis; it is corroborated second-hand by Lobel 2013:287, who cites Sullivan 1986:11 for Maguindanaon phonemic stress in contrast to Maranao. Held Allison 1979 and Juanmarti 1906 are silent; Zorc 1993's accent typology omits Maguindanao. The only contrary statement is Porter 1903's soldier's-primer rule of thumb (penultimate accent by syllable count), which carries little weight against Eck's transcribed contrasts (/'ipu/ vs /i'ga/, /la'nun/, /pu'ting/).
